newsitem.title: LATVIA: Latvian PM recalled to power, vows more reforms.
newsitem.headline: Latvian PM recalled to power, vows more reforms.

text.p: Latvian President Guntis Ulmanis on Wednesday asked former prime minister Andris Shkele, who quit last week, to form a new government for the Baltic state.
Shkele quit nine days ago in fury at Ulmanis, who had appealed to parliament to reject the premier's choice of finance minister, Vassily Melnik.
"I have been invited by the president to form a new government," Shkele told reporters after meeting Ulmanis for more than an hour.
Shkele said he would continue to carry out reforms in Latvia, which quit the Soviet Union in 1991 and wants to attract foreign investment and boost its links with the West.
"The government programme will not change in any way. We will have to formulate it more precisely," Shkele said.
Ulmanis asked parliament to reject the finance minister after reports that the prosecutor's office had investigated Melnik under anti-corruption laws.
State prosecutors confirmed the reports but said they found no wrong doing. Melnik was later backed by parliament but resigned just two days after Shkele announced he was quitting.
Shkele, a non-party businessman, formed his first government at the end of 1995 in the wake of a banking crisis that caused thousands of Latvia's 2.7 million people to lose their savings.
He said that putting together a new administration would be a tough task. The new government will have to be approved by parliament.
Latvia's 100-seat parliament is split between 12 parties and around 10 independent deputies. No single party has anywhere near a majority.
Shkele's former eight-party governing coalition had the support of around 70 members of parliament.
His rival for the prime minister's post was Economics Minister Guntar Krasts, who was proposed by the third-largest party in the former coalition.
Ulmanis asked Shkele to form a new government after several days of talks with large and small political parties.
"As a result of these consultations I consider that the majority of parties are ready to support Shkele," Ulmanis said.
The row over Melnik did not cause a long-term rift between Ulmanis and Shkele. The two leaders later announced they had settled their differences.
